name: Rafael Moneo
bio:
Rafael Moneo (born 1937) is a Spanish architect from Tudela who graduated from the Technical University of Madrid in 1961. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1996, the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 2003 and the Venice Biennale's Golden Lion in 2021. The jury of the 2012 Prince of Asturias Award called his architecture "serene and meticulous", with interiors that act as settings for great works of culture.

The National Museum of Roman Art in Mérida (1986) was built to show finds from Augusta Emerita, the Roman colony that is one of Spain's largest archaeological sites. The Kursaal in San Sebastián (1999) is two "cubes" by the sea, each an inner structure wrapped in double panels of translucent glass, with a terrace between them looking over Zurriola beach and the river mouth. In Los Angeles, the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels (2002), chosen from 38 entries, replaced a cathedral damaged in the 1994 Northridge earthquake and drew controversy over its design and cost. He also extended the Prado Museum in Madrid (2007). Rafael Moneo's projects are studied for how new buildings can sit calmly beside old ones.

name: SANAA
bio:
SANAA (Sejima and Nishizawa and Associates) is an architecture firm based in Tokyo, founded in 1995 by Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa. The two partners shared the Pritzker Prize in 2010, and the firm's buildings stand in Japan, Europe, the United States and Australia.

The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa (2004) holds galleries of many sizes and kinds of light, from bright rooms under glass ceilings to rooms with no daylight, inside a round glass wall that Sejima bent gently towards an oval. The Rolex Learning Center (2010), the main library of the EPFL in Lausanne. At the Louvre-Lens (2012), the museum is a string of five low buildings, meant to blend into the land: the central one has glass walls, the others are clad in polished aluminium that gives a blurred reflection of the surroundings. Other SANAA projects include the Glass Pavilion, Toledo Museum of Art (2006), Dior Omotesando in Tokyo (2003) and the Art Gallery of New South Wales, North Building (Sydney Modern, Naala Nura) (2022). SANAA's buildings are studied for lightness, glass and the way a building can step back into its setting.

name: Arne Jacobsen
bio:
Arne Jacobsen (1902–1971) was a Danish architect and furniture designer, born in Copenhagen, who designed whole buildings down to their furniture. Many of his best-known designs, including the three-legged Ant chair and the Egg and Swan chairs, were made for his own buildings. As a Jewish Dane in the Second World War he fled to Sweden, rowing across the Øresund with help from the Danish resistance.

The Bellavista housing in Klampenborg (1934) is built of concrete, steel and glass, with open plans and no ornament. Skovshoved Petrol Station nearby (1936) is known for its projecting oval canopy, nicknamed "the Mushroom". With Erik Møller he designed Aarhus City Hall (1941), a concrete building faced in grey Norwegian marble whose 60-metre tower was added after public pressure. The SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen (1960), called the world's first designer hotel: Jacobsen designed everything from the building to the ashtrays and airport buses. At St Catherine's College, Oxford (1962), his buildings of glass, brick and concrete keep the traditional plan around a quadrangle and are listed Grade I. Arne Jacobsen's buildings are studied for treating architecture and furniture as one design.

name: James Stirling
bio:
James Stirling (1926–1992) was a British architect, born in Glasgow, whose work moved from hard-edged, technical modernism to colourful postmodern buildings that borrow from the past. He worked with James Gowan from 1956 to 1963 and with Michael Wilford from 1971 until his death, and he won the Pritzker Prize in 1981. Britain's annual Stirling Prize for architecture is named after him.

With Gowan he designed the Leicester University Engineering Building (1963), noted for its technical, geometric character and for being worked out in axonometric drawings seen from above and below. Alone he designed the History Faculty Building, Cambridge (1968). The Neue Staatsgalerie in Stuttgart (1984) plays on the plan of Berlin's neoclassical Altes Museum: a public path and ramp wind around a central open-air rotunda, and sandstone and travertine meet green steel frames and bright pink and blue handrails. No 1 Poultry in London (1997), finished after his death by Wilford, has bands of pink and yellow stone and became the youngest building in England listed Grade II*. James Stirling's projects are studied for bold form and their dialogue with history.

name: Pier Luigi Nervi
bio:
Pier Luigi Nervi (1891–1979) was an Italian engineer and architect known for his inventive use of reinforced concrete, above all thin shells, ribs and vaults that let him do away with columns. Born in Sondrio, he graduated in engineering from Bologna in 1913, taught in Rome and was a Norton Professor at Harvard. He held that intuition mattered as much as mathematics, and joined simple geometry to prefabrication.

His early works include the Stadio Artemio Franchi in Florence (1931), and his concrete aircraft hangars of the 1930s developed the precast ribs and modular building he used for the rest of his life. The Palazzetto dello Sport in Rome (1957) covers its arena with a ribbed concrete dome 61 metres across, made of 1,620 prefabricated pieces braced by flying buttresses and raised in 40 days. He worked with Marcel Breuer and Bernard Zehrfuss on the UNESCO Headquarters in Paris (1958) and with Gio Ponti on the Pirelli Tower in Milan. The Paul VI Audience Hall in Vatican City (1971) seats 6,300 people under his concrete structure. Pier Luigi Nervi's buildings are studied for structure that becomes the architecture itself.

name: Auguste Perret
bio:
Auguste Perret (1874–1954) was a French architect and a pioneer of building with reinforced concrete. Trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, he kept the order and symmetry of classical architecture but let the concrete frame show. Le Corbusier worked in his office from 1908 to 1910, and in 2005 his post-war rebuilding of Le Havre was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

His first important project, the apartment building at 25 bis rue Franklin in Paris (1904), left its concrete structure visible as part of the façade instead of hiding it. The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées (1913), which he took over from Henry van de Velde, is often called the first Art Deco building in Paris. Notre-Dame du Raincy (1923) is a concrete church filled with stained glass by Marguerite Huré. The Perret Tower in Grenoble (1925), built for an exhibition of hydropower and tourism, was the first concrete tower of its kind. In Le Havre, St. Joseph's Church (1957) raises a 107-metre lantern tower that acts as a beacon seen from the sea. Auguste Perret's buildings are studied for how a concrete frame can carry classical proportion.

name: Carlos Raúl Villanueva
bio:
Carlos Raúl Villanueva (1900–1975) was a Venezuelan modernist architect, born in London and trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, who helped modernise Caracas and Maracay. He believed painting and sculpture should be joined with architecture, a "synthesis of the arts". His masterwork, the University City of Caracas, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

He worked on the campus of the Central University of Venezuela from 1944 to 1970. In its Aula Magna (1953), Alexander Calder's "Floating Clouds" hang from the ceiling: coloured panels that are both art and part of the hall's acoustics. The campus also holds the Covered Plaza, University City of Caracas (1954). In housing, his El Silencio redevelopment in Caracas provided 7,797 apartments, and he later designed the 23 de Enero Superblocks (1957). The Jesús Soto Museum of Modern Art in Ciudad Bolívar (1973), a late work, links six simple buildings by covered walkways around a garden of art; Villanueva wanted it "so pure that there is no longer an appreciable difference between roofs, walls and natural spaces". Carlos Raúl Villanueva's buildings are studied for joining art, landscape and modern architecture.

name: MVRDV
bio:
MVRDV is an architecture and urban design practice in Rotterdam, founded in 1993 by Winy Maas, Jacob van Rijs and Nathalie de Vries, whose surnames make up its name. It also has offices in Berlin, New York, Paris and Shanghai, and much of its research, in books such as FARMAX, is about density in cities.

Its early built works include the WoZoCo housing in Amsterdam (1997) and the Netherlands Pavilion, Expo 2000 in Hanover. The Markthal in Rotterdam (2014) wraps 228 apartments in a horseshoe-shaped arch of grey stone over a large covered market; it won several awards but not universal praise. The Tianjin Binhai Library in China (2017), nicknamed "The Eye", lines its interior with floor-to-ceiling terraced bookshelves around a glowing sphere that holds a 110-seat auditorium. The Depot Boijmans van Beuningen in Rotterdam (2021), the world's first art store open to the public, is a 39.5-metre bowl clad in 1,664 mirror panels that reflect the city around it, and shows more than 150,000 works the museum had no room to display before. MVRDV's projects are studied for density, stacking and bold public form.

name: Paul Rudolph
bio:
Paul Rudolph (1918–1997) was an American architect known first for light, inventive houses in Florida and then for heavy, sculptural concrete buildings of American brutalism. He studied under Walter Gropius at Harvard, became an early figure of the Sarasota School of Architecture, and chaired Yale's Department of Architecture from 1958 to 1965, where his students included Norman Foster and Richard Rogers.

In Sarasota, the Umbrella House (Hiss Residence) (1953) shades the house, patio and pool with a latticed second roof floating above the first, letting air move to cool it. The Walker Guest House on Sanibel Island (1953) rests on a raised steel frame with movable wooden panels that open the rooms to the outdoors. The Yale Art and Architecture Building in New Haven (1963), a spatially complex concrete structure, is his best-known brutalist work, with the Boston Government Service Center (1971). Late in his career he worked in Asia, and the Lippo Centre in Hong Kong (1988) was the culmination of his ideas about reflective glass. Paul Rudolph's buildings are studied for their complex sections and for the way they shape light and shade.

name: Paulo Mendes da Rocha
bio:
Paulo Mendes da Rocha (1928–2021) was a Brazilian architect who worked almost only in Brazil and is widely credited with renewing São Paulo through its cultural buildings. A graduate of Mackenzie Presbyterian University (1954) and a professor at the University of São Paulo's architecture school until 1998, he was influenced by Vilanova Artigas and the Paulista School. Much of his work is in concrete, an approach some call "Brazilian Brutalism". He won the Pritzker Prize in 2006 and the Venice Biennale's Golden Lion for lifetime achievement in 2016.

His renovation of the Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo (1998), the city's oldest art museum, helped make it one of Brazil's most active cultural institutions. In São Paulo he also designed MuBE – Brazilian Museum of Sculpture (1995) and SESC 24 de Maio (2017). In Lisbon, the new National Coach Museum (2015), designed with the Ricardo Bak Gordon studio and the engineer Rui Furtado, holds most of the royal coach collection and has been Portugal's most visited national museum. Paulo Mendes da Rocha's buildings are studied for bold concrete structure and open public space.

name: Peter Zumthor
bio:
Peter Zumthor (born 1943) is a Swiss architect known for a small number of carefully made buildings; on his 80th birthday the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung called him "the great magician of minimalism". The son of a Basel cabinet-maker, he trained as a carpenter and works from a small studio of about 30 people in Haldenstein near Chur. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2009 and the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 2013.

The Saint Benedict Chapel in Sumvitg (1988) is among his early works in the mountains of Graubünden. Therme Vals (1996), a spa built over the only thermal springs in that canton, is often described as cave-like. The Kunsthaus Bregenz (1997) is a shimmering cube of glass, steel and cast concrete on the shore of Lake Constance; the two won the 1998 Carlsberg Architectural Prize. The Kolumba Museum in Cologne (2007) is the city's diocesan art museum, and the Bruder Klaus Field Chapel (2007) stands on a farm near Wachendorf. The Steilneset Memorial in Vardø (2011) remembers the victims of the witch trials there. Peter Zumthor's buildings are studied for material, light and the experience of being inside them.

name: Steven Holl
bio:
Steven Holl (born 1947) is a New York-based American architect and watercolourist whose buildings are shaped around the experience of light, material and movement. With Juhani Pallasmaa and Alberto Pérez-Gómez he wrote Questions of Perception: Phenomenology of Architecture (1994), and he has taught at Columbia University since 1981. He received the AIA Gold Medal in 2012 and the Praemium Imperiale in 2014.

The Chapel of St. Ignatius in Seattle (1997), "seven bottles of light in a stone box" in Holl's words, colours the daylight by bouncing it off painted baffles and through tinted glass. Kiasma in Helsinki (1998), the city's museum of contemporary art, takes its name from the Greek chiasma, "crossing". For the Bloch Building, Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City (2007), designed with Chris McVoy, five glass "lenses" rise above mostly underground galleries and let daylight reach the art, against the usual caution of museums. Linked Hybrid in Beijing (2009), 750 apartments with shops, a cinema and schools, is heated and cooled by geothermal wells. Steven Holl's projects are studied for how light and the way a visitor moves through space can lead a design.

name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
bio:
Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868–1928) was a Scottish architect, designer and watercolourist from Glasgow who blended his Scottish background with the flourish of Art Nouveau and the simplicity of Japanese forms. With his wife Margaret Macdonald, her sister Frances Macdonald and Herbert MacNair he formed "The Four", leading figures of the Glasgow Style, and their work influenced Art Nouveau and the Secession movement across Europe. Late in life he gave up architecture for watercolour painting.

He studied in the evenings at the Glasgow School of Art and later designed its building (1909), which was badly damaged by fire in 2014 and destroyed by a second fire in 2018. His Glasgow Herald offices of 1895 are now The Lighthouse (Glasgow Herald Building), a design centre. The Willow Tearooms in Glasgow (1903) were made for the tea-room owner Catherine Cranston, and Scotland Street School (1906) has been a museum since 1990. The House for an Art Lover in Glasgow (1996) was built between 1989 and 1996 from a design he and Margaret Macdonald drew in 1901. Charles Rennie Mackintosh's buildings are studied for treating architecture, interiors and craft as one.

name: Denys Lasdun
bio:
Denys Lasdun (1914–2001) was an English architect, hailed as "the greatest English architect of the early heroic modern period", whose best-known buildings are landmarks of British brutalism. He studied at the Architectural Association in London. His typical style combined cubic towers, bare concrete and jutting decks, and he received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1977.

Keeling House in London's Bethnal Green (1957) is one of his "cluster blocks": four blocks of maisonettes grouped around a central service tower. The Royal College of Physicians in Regent's Park (1964), seen as his breakthrough, is listed Grade I. At the University of East Anglia Ziggurats (Norfolk and Suffolk Terraces) in Norwich (1968), stepped, glazed student rooms rise beside classrooms and laboratories linked by walkways. The Royal National Theatre on London's South Bank (1976), his best-known work, is built of pale concrete meant to match the stone of nearby Waterloo Bridge and Somerset House. It is now listed Grade II*, though the future King Charles once compared it to a nuclear power station. Denys Lasdun's buildings are studied for horizontal terraces, public decks and the drama of concrete.

name: Diébédo Francis Kéré
bio:
Diébédo Francis Kéré (born 1965) is a Burkinabé-German architect, born in the village of Gando in Burkina Faso and based in Berlin, known for sustainable buildings made with local materials and with the people who will use them. He studied architecture at the Technische Universität Berlin, founded Kéré Architecture in 2005, and in 2022 became the first African-born architect to win the Pritzker Prize.

His first building, the Gando Primary School (2001), has mud-brick walls under a wide, raised metal roof that keeps off the rain and lets air flow through to cool the classrooms; villagers helped build it, and it won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2004. The Dano Secondary School (2007) is built of local laterite stone and faces east–west to cut the sun on its walls. The Centre for Earth Architecture in Mopti, Mali (2010), uses the same techniques as the region's great earthen mosques. The Opera Village (Operndorf Afrika) in Laongo (2011), begun with the German director Christoph Schlingensief, includes a school, workshops and a medical centre. Diébédo Francis Kéré's projects are studied for climate-wise design built with local skills.

name: Eliel Saarinen
bio:
Eliel Saarinen (1873–1950) was a Finnish-American architect whose early work defined Finnish National Romanticism and whose later teaching shaped American design. From 1896 to 1905 he worked in Helsinki with Herman Gesellius and Armas Lindgren. His entry for the 1922 Chicago Tribune Tower competition won second place and, though never built, helped shape Art Deco skyscrapers. He then moved to the United States, designed the campus of the Cranbrook Educational Community in Michigan, and became president of the Cranbrook Academy of Art in 1932. He was the father of the architect Eero Saarinen.

Helsinki Central Station (1919), designed in 1904 and clad in granite, is known for its clock tower and Emil Wikström's "Lantern Bearers" statues, and marks the peak of his National Romantic style. Lahti Town Hall (1912) and Joensuu Town Hall (1914) come from the same Finnish years. In the United States he designed the Des Moines Art Center (1948), and Christ Church Lutheran in Minneapolis (1949), designed with Eero, was his last completed building and is now a National Historic Landmark. Eliel Saarinen's buildings are studied for the move from national romanticism to modern design.

name: Geoffrey Bawa
bio:
Geoffrey Bawa (1919–2003) was a Sri Lankan architect whose buildings joined modern design to local materials, crafts and landscape. Born in Colombo, he studied English and law at Cambridge before training at the Architectural Association in London, where he earned his diploma in 1956. With artists such as Ena de Silva, Barbara Sansoni and Laki Senanayake he helped spark a new interest in indigenous materials and crafts.

At Lunuganga, an abandoned rubber estate on the south-west coast that he bought for himself, he set out to make an Italian garden out of a tropical wilderness. The Bentota Beach Hotel (1969) joined modern rooms to forms and materials of its setting and influenced later resorts in the country. Seema Malaka in Colombo (1976), a temple rebuilt on three platforms in Beira Lake joined by pontoon bridges, draws on the ancient forest monasteries of Anuradhapura and Ritigala. The Parliament of Sri Lanka (1982) stands on an island in a lake at Kotte, and Heritance Kandalama (1994) wraps a hotel around a cliff, entered through a cave-like porch. Geoffrey Bawa's buildings are studied for their response to climate, landscape and craft.

name: Harry Seidler
bio:
Harry Seidler (1923–2006) was an Austrian-born Australian architect, seen as the first to fully express the principles of the Bauhaus in Australia. Born in Vienna to a Jewish family, he fled the Nazis to Britain, where he was interned as an enemy alien, then studied at Harvard under Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer, becoming Breuer's first assistant in New York. He received the Royal Australian Institute of Architects Gold Medal in 1976 and the RIBA Royal Gold Medal.

The Rose Seidler House in Wahroonga (1950), built for his parents in Sydney bushland, was the first completely modern house in Australia to express the Bauhaus approach and won the Sulman Award. With the Italian engineer Pier Luigi Nervi he designed Australia Square in Sydney (1967), then the world's tallest lightweight concrete building, and the MLC Centre (1977), a white octagonal tower on eight tapering corner columns that was Sydney's tallest office building until 1992. Blues Point Tower (1962) and Horizon Apartments (1998) show the influence of the painter Theo van Doesburg. Harry Seidler's buildings are studied for structure and for modernism adapted to the Australian climate.

name: Jørn Utzon
bio:
Jørn Utzon (1918–2008) was a Danish architect best known for the Sydney Opera House and for what he called "additive architecture": buildings made from repeated parts that grow, he said, like a tree. He trained at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts and was influenced early by Gunnar Asplund and Alvar Aalto. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2003.

Utzon won the 1957 competition for the Sydney Opera House (1973), but in 1966, after a dispute over the roof, he resigned, left Australia and never returned to see it finished. When it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, he was the second architect, after Oscar Niemeyer, to see a work so listed in his lifetime. In Denmark, the Kingo Houses in Helsingør (1958) set dozens of L-shaped courtyard homes, modelled on traditional farmhouses, like "flowers on the branch of a cherry tree". Bagsværd Church near Copenhagen (1976) is lit by daylight under a concrete ceiling of soft, rounded vaults. Can Lis on Mallorca (1972) was shaped by local materials and climate. Jørn Utzon's buildings are studied for their growth from simple parts and their tie to landscape.

name: Mimar Sinan
bio:
Mimar Sinan (c. 1490–1588) was chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for nearly 50 years, serving the sultans Suleiman the Magnificent, Selim II and Murad III. Before he was an architect he was a Janissary officer, and on campaign he learned to build fortifications, roads, bridges and aqueducts. As chief architect he oversaw all building work in the empire and was responsible for more than 300 major structures.

Sinan studied the great domed buildings before him, including the Hagia Sophia, and returned again and again to the large central dome. The Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul (1548), which he called a work of his apprenticeship, sets its dome on four equal half-domes carried by four free-standing piers. The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (1557), his most famous work, was finished when he was about 70. His masterpiece is held to be the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne (1575), a UNESCO World Heritage Site with its complex since 2011. The Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge over the Drina at Višegrad (1577) is also on the World Heritage list. Mimar Sinan's buildings are studied for structure, the central dome and the planning of whole complexes.

name: Ricardo Bofill
bio:
Ricardo Bofill (1939–2022) was a Spanish architect from Barcelona who founded the Taller de Arquitectura in 1963 and grew it into an international architecture and urban design practice. His early housing experimented with three-dimensional modular geometry; his later, monumental work in France made him one of Europe's best-known postmodern architects. Bjarke Ingels has named La Fábrica and Walden 7 as influences.

La Muralla Roja in Calp (1973), "the Red Wall", is a postmodern apartment complex of about fifty homes. Walden 7 in Sant Just Desvern (1975) is a "vertical labyrinth" of 18 towers around seven linked courtyards, with flats made of 28-square-metre modules that can be combined as families change. Next door, La Fábrica (1975) is a former cement factory that his practice turned into offices and living space. Les Espaces d'Abraxas near Paris (1983) puts housing in grand Roman, Greek and Baroque forms, which critics called "a unique combination of the romantic sublime and totalitarian awe"; it has served as a backdrop for films such as Brazil and The Hunger Games. Ricardo Bofill's buildings are studied for modular housing and for monumental classical forms made in concrete.

name: Balkrishna Doshi
bio:
Balkrishna Doshi (1927–2023) was an Indian architect, born in Pune, who pioneered modernist and brutalist architecture in India and became known for low-income housing and for designs that build in sustainability. He worked with Le Corbusier in Paris from 1951 to 1954 and with Louis Kahn on the Indian Institute of Management in Ahmedabad, and he opened his own studio, Vastu-Shilpa, in 1955. In 2018 he became the first Indian architect to win the Pritzker Prize.

Many of his buildings are in Ahmedabad, including CEPT University (1966), Premabhai Hall (1972) and his own studio, Sangath (1981). The Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (1983) is among his best-known campuses. Aranya Low Cost Housing in Indore (1989) won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. Amdavad ni Gufa in Ahmedabad (1995), built to show the work of the artist M. F. Husain, is a cave-like underground gallery: its roof is a cluster of linked domes covered in a mosaic of broken crockery and waste tiles, held up inside by irregular, tree-like columns. Balkrishna Doshi's buildings are studied for low-cost housing, climate and sustainable design.

name: Carlo Scarpa
bio:
Carlo Scarpa (1906–1978) was an Italian architect and designer from Venice whose work drew on the materials, landscape and history of Venetian culture, and on that of Japan. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Venice but refused to sit the state licensing exam, so he could never use the title "architetto"; clients called him "Professore". He taught drawing and interior design at the Venice architecture school from the late 1940s until his death, and early in his career he designed glass with the makers of Murano.

Much of his work reshapes existing places. In Venice he designed the Olivetti Showroom (1958) and renewed the ground floor and garden of the Fondazione Querini Stampalia (Scarpa ground floor and garden) (1963). At the Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975), his restoration between 1959 and 1973 reworked both the old castle and the display of its art. The Brion Cemetery at San Vito d'Altivole (1978), a group of concrete buildings with distinctive detailing set in gardens with water, is also where he is buried. Carlo Scarpa's work is studied for detail and the dialogue between new and old.

name: Christian de Portzamparc
bio:
Christian de Portzamparc (born 1944) is a French architect and urbanist, born in Casablanca and trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. In 1994, at the age of 50, he became the first French architect to win the Pritzker Prize. In the 1980s he developed the "open block", a new way of shaping city blocks that he has since used for a whole Paris neighbourhood, Quartier Masséna.

The Cité de la musique in Paris (1995), one of President Mitterrand's Grands Projets, brings together a concert hall, a museum of musical instruments and a music library in the Parc de la Villette. The LVMH Tower in New York (1999) is the best-known of his prismatic towers. The Philharmonie Luxembourg (2005) is wrapped in 823 white steel columns set in three or four rows. One57 in New York (2014) was, for a few months, the city's tallest residential building. The Cidade das Artes in Rio de Janeiro (2013), with 1,780 seats, is South America's largest modern concert hall, though it cost about six times its budget. Christian de Portzamparc's projects are studied for the open block and for sculptural towers.

name: Coop Himmelb(l)au
bio:
Coop Himmelb(l)au is an architecture, urban planning, design and art practice founded in Vienna in 1968 by Wolf D. Prix, Helmut Swiczinsky and Michael Holzer. Its name is a pun on "sky building" and "sky blue". Its work was shown in the Museum of Modern Art's 1988 "Deconstructivist Architecture" exhibition, curated by Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley, and the firm has been counted among the deconstructivists ever since.

At the Groninger Museum (1994), it designed a pale blue deconstructivist pavilion beside others by Philippe Starck and Alessandro Mendini. Gasometer B in Vienna (2001) turns a 1890s gas holder into flats, offices and shops. BMW Welt in Munich (2007), a delivery and exhibition centre with an 800-kilowatt solar plant on its roof. The Busan Cinema Center in South Korea (2011) holds the Guinness World Record for the longest cantilevered roof. The Musée des Confluences in Lyon (2014) has been likened to a floating crystal cloud of stainless steel and glass, and the European Central Bank in Frankfurt (2014) joins twin office towers to a renovated 1920s market hall. Coop Himmelb(l)au's projects are studied for dynamic, fragmented forms and long-span structures.

name: Edward Durell Stone
bio:
Edward Durell Stone (1902–1978) was an American architect who began as an early champion of the International Style and became known for the formal, highly decorative buildings he designed in the 1950s and 1960s. Born in Fayetteville, Arkansas, he was principal designer of Radio City Music Hall and, from 1936, associate architect with Philip Goodwin on the new Museum of Modern Art in New York. His US Embassy in New Delhi (1959), a temple-like pavilion on a raised podium that Frank Lloyd Wright called one of the most beautiful buildings he had seen, made his career.

His first independent commission, the Richard H. Mandel House in New York State (1935), comes from his International Style years. His later, more ornamental buildings include the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico (1965) and the Kennedy Center in Washington (1971). He also designed the W. E. B. Du Bois Library at the University of Massachusetts Amherst (1974) and the Aiwan-e-Sadr (Presidential Palace) in Islamabad (1981). Edward Durell Stone's buildings are studied for his turn from modernist plainness to symmetry and ornament.

name: Félix Candela
bio:
Félix Candela (1910–1997) was a Spanish-Mexican architect, born in Madrid, known for thin reinforced-concrete shells, called cascarones, often shaped as hyperbolic paraboloids that join form and structural efficiency. After fighting in the Spanish Civil War and being held in a camp at Perpignan, he emigrated to Mexico at 29. Many of his larger projects came from the Mexican government, and from 1971 to 1978 he taught at the University of Illinois at Chicago.

The Cosmic Rays Pavilion at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (1951), is an early work. Los Manantiales Restaurant in Mexico City (1958) is roofed with hyperbolic paraboloid shells. The Palacio de los Deportes in Mexico City (1968), built for that year's Olympic basketball tournament, covers a round hall with a dome 120 metres across, made of aluminium hyperbolic paraboloids clad in copper-sheathed plywood and carried on steel arches. At the age of 87 he designed the thin-shell roof of L'Oceanogràfic Restaurant in Valencia (2003), with the engineers Alberto Domingo and Carlos Lázaro, in a form that echoes Los Manantiales. Félix Candela's buildings are studied for how geometry lets thin concrete span great distances.

name: gmp Architekten
bio:
gmp (von Gerkan, Marg and Partners) is a German architecture practice based in Hamburg, founded in 1965 by Meinhard von Gerkan and Volkwin Marg. In its first year it won the international competition for Berlin's Tegel Airport, which gave it international recognition. It now has more than 300 staff in 13 offices, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hanoi, and has worked on close to 500 buildings in 23 countries, from airports and stations to a long list of stadiums.

Tegel Airport, Terminal A in Berlin (1974) was that first winning design. In Vietnam, gmp designed the Vietnam National Convention Center (2006) and the Hanoi Museum (2010) in Hanoi. For the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa it designed Moses Mabhida Stadium in Durban (2009), whose 46,000-square-metre roof of Teflon-coated glass-fibre membrane is hung from a great arch on steel cables and glows when the stadium is lit, and Cape Town Stadium (2009), working with local architects. Baku Crystal Hall in Azerbaijan (2012) followed. gmp's projects are studied for how large public buildings such as airports and stadiums can be planned around structure and crowds.

name: Hans Scharoun
bio:
Hans Scharoun (1893–1972) was a German architect from Bremen and an important figure of organic and expressionist architecture. In 1919 he joined Bruno Taut's expressionist group, the Glass Chain, and the theories of Hugo Häring later took him in a new direction. He stayed in Germany through the Nazi years, building only a few family houses, and several of his most important buildings were finished after his death.

Villa Schminke in Löbau (1933), one of those houses, is open to the public. After the war, the Geschwister-Scholl-Schule in Lünen (1962) was planned like a small city. The Berliner Philharmonie (1963), home of the Berlin Philharmonic and considered his best work, places the orchestra podium near the centre, with the audience rising around it on irregular terraces under ceilings layered like a tent. The Berlin State Library (Haus Potsdamer Straße) (1978), the Scharoun Theatre Wolfsburg (1973) and the German Maritime Museum (Scharoun building) in Bremerhaven (1975) were all completed after he died. Hans Scharoun's buildings are studied for the way each space is shaped by its use.

facts.claim: 20 September 1893 – 25 November 1972; German architect born in Bremen; important exponent of organic and expressionist architecture

Berliner Philharmonie (1956–63): "Scharoun's best work"; spectators rise in irregular terraces around the music podium; ceiling layered like a tent-like firmament
Home of the Berlin Philharmonic
Finished after his death: German Maritime Museum, Bremerhaven; the theatre in Wolfsburg; the Berlin State Library

name: John Burgee
bio:
John Burgee (born 1933) is an American architect known for his contributions to postmodern architecture as Philip Johnson's partner from 1967 to 1991, in the firm Johnson/Burgee Architects. A 1956 graduate of the University of Notre Dame's architecture school, he eased Johnson out of the firm in 1991; it went bankrupt soon after, which in effect ended his design career.

The IDS Center in Minneapolis (1972) centres on the Crystal Court, a seven-storey covered space linked by skyways to four blocks. Pennzoil Place in Houston (1975) was one of their landmark towers. PPG Place in Pittsburgh (1984) wraps a neo-Gothic office complex in 19,750 pieces of glass for a glass company, and the AT&T Building (550 Madison Avenue) in New York (1984) became a symbol of postmodernism. The firm moved into its own almost elliptical Lipstick Building in New York (1986). In Madrid, the twin towers of the Gate of Europe (1996) lean towards each other at 15 degrees, the first inclined skyscrapers in the world. John Burgee's buildings are studied for corporate postmodernism and its historical references.
